newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Experts see lower rates with UK council.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Experts see lower rates with UK council.

text.p: British interest rates are expected to be lower in the long term under the country's new rate-setting body, a Reuters survey showed.

Seventeen out of 21 contributors to the poll, conducted on Tuesday, said the monetary policy committee which is taking over the task of setting rates from the Chancellor of the Exchequer would result in lower interest rates.
Two said base rates would be higher in the long term, while two said it would make no difference.

"There is a good chance the committee will build up a reputation for good policy decisions and in the long term this will translate into lower interest rates," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.

On May 6, just five days into office, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced the Bank of England would be given freedom to set interest rates. Britain's financial markets surged in approval of the new finance minister's move.

The council's deliberations replace the monthly meetings between Eddie George, Governor of the Bank of England, and the incumbent Chancellor. Under the old regime, former Chancellor Clarke would make a decision on rates straight after the meeting.
Brown set up a nine-person monetary council and gave the Bank an inbuilt majority of five members. The other four will be "outsiders" -- economists from academia and industry.
Of the outsiders, only Charles Goodhart from the London School of Economics and Willem Buiter from Cambridge University will sit on the committee immediately.
British Airways economist DeAnne Julius and the Treasury's Alan Budd will join later as will a second deputy Bank governor, yet to be appointed.
In terms of expertise, competence and credibility, the council members earned an "approval rating" of three or higher on a scale of one to five from all contributors who responded to this question.
Three declined to pass judgement, saying it was too early to tell.

The two respondents who allocated the highest rating of five said they felt the system now being put in place was non-political, would best serve to promote stable economic growth and was better than the previous one.
But the 16 respondents who rated the new committee at three or four said the new system needed time before it could be completely trusted.

"There are some doves and some hawks -- it's neutral. But it will take time to see the effects of their decisions and more time for them to build up credibility to the extent that the (U.S.) Federal Reserve has," said Mark Geddes, Treasury economist at ABN AMRO.

Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, has doubts about the framework of the new system and believes along with one other contributor that it will make no difference to base rates in the long term.

"With credibility the government can win lower interest rates, they dont need an independent central bank for that," he said. "And there is no concrete framework for their choice of who sits on the council. It's a mishmash of academics and practitioners."
